stemBlocks.value: Using a ruler, a pencil and a pair of compasses, construct the right-angled triangle ABC such that AB = 5 cm, ∠ABC = 90° and ∠BAC = 60°.
Think first: Both required angles, 90° and 60°, are standard compass constructions built on the ends of AB.

stemBlocks.altText: Source visual for edmar-csec-p161-q18 from workbook page 161.

solutionSteps.instruction: Construct a perpendicular to AB at B.

contentBlocks.value: Equal arcs each side of B along AB, then equal larger arcs from those points crossing above B

solutionSteps.instruction: Construct a 60° angle at A on the same side of AB.

contentBlocks.value: Centre A, arc cutting AB; same radius from that point cuts the arc; join A to it

solutionSteps.instruction: Mark C where the two arms meet and join AC.

strategyBlocks.value: Draw AB = 5 cm, construct 90° at B and 60° at A on the same side, and mark C where the two arms cross.

finalAnswerBlocks.value: A correctly constructed right-angled triangle ABC with AB = 5 cm, ∠ABC = 90° and ∠BAC = 60°. Accuracy checks: BC ≈ 8.7 cm, AC = 10 cm and ∠ACB = 30°.

whyThisWorks.value: Fixing a side and both angles at its ends (ASA) determines a triangle uniquely, so the two arms can only meet in one place. Because the triangle is right-angled, the tangent and cosine ratios give exact predicted lengths, turning an accuracy question into something you can verify numerically instead of trusting your eye.

commonErrors.misconception: Building the 60° at B and the 90° at A, which reverses the triangle.
commonErrors.correctiveNote: Avoid this: Building the 60° at B and the 90° at A, which reverses the triangle.

commonErrors.misconception: Drawing the two angles on opposite sides of AB, so the arms never meet.
commonErrors.correctiveNote: Avoid this: Drawing the two angles on opposite sides of AB, so the arms never meet.

examTip.value: Before drawing, sketch the triangle roughly and label the angles — it takes ten seconds and prevents the swapped-angle error that costs full marks.
